name: Hassan Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Harbour Street job centre, a small branch in a seaside town, handling jobseeker allowance claims. Mornings I work the claims queue, afternoons I do appointments with people who've just lost work, a lot of them from the fish processing plant that shut in the summer. I'm quick on the computer but I still trip over the rules, like when savings count against a claim, and Anita, my team leader, catches me on that weekly. I live with my boyfriend Tomas, who's a physiotherapist at the hospital up the hill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Constantly. I've got my own set of prompts for the AI assistant we're allowed to use, one for summarising a claimant's work history, one for drafting a plain-English letter. I'm on the office's digital pilot group, which mostly means I'm the one who fixes the printer as well. Anita calls me the office's teenager, even though I'm twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest. I like the tools. But I can see that happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful even if they're not magic. I'd probably post a little thread about the three prompts that save me an hour a day. Somebody in the regional office would share it and I'd be insufferable for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. My job's steady, Tomas's job is steady, and our rent is reasonable for a seaside town out of season. The only thing that'd bother me is if I'd backed the wrong horse by being the AI guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my prompt library and share it with the team. I'd ask Anita to put me forward for the regional digital champion role, which is a small step up. And I'd get the savings rules nailed, properly, so she stops catching me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly bored. Like a party that turned out to be a quiet drink. Fine, just not what I'd hoped for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being the AI guy cost you if it fizzled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some credibility, maybe. I'd rather be the person who tried the new tool and shrugged than the one who never looked up from the old form. Nobody gets sacked for being curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any money worries in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. We've got about four months saved and we're trying to get to six. The car's old, so that's the next big bill, not my job.

say: I'd say the AI tools are **still useful** even without big change.
I'd post a thread sharing my **three prompts** that save an hour daily.
think: My job and my partner's are **both steady**, so I'd be fine.
My only worry is having **backed the wrong horse** as the office AI enthusiast.
do: Keep building and sharing my **prompt library** with the team.
Ask my team leader to nominate me as **digital champion**.
Master the **savings rules** so my mistakes stop.
feel: **Calm** and slightly **bored**, like a party that became a quiet drink.
S0.quote: I'd rather be the person who tried the new tool and shrugged than the one who never looked up from the old form.
fieldNote: He is the **most enthusiastic** AI user in his office and enjoys the role.
His household has **two steady incomes**, which gives real security.
His **skill gap** is in benefit rules, not technology.

steps.text: Share his prompt library with the Harbour Street team
Ask Anita to nominate him as regional digital champion
Keep saving towards six months for the old car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I half expect. And I'd be right in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to fix the boring parts and spend more time with people. And I'd say, loudly, that the savings should go back into the service, not into cuts. I'd say that at the union too, even though people there think I'm a bit of a traitor for liking the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm better placed than most juniors. I'm already the one people come to. But I know being good with tools doesn't save you if the tools do your job, so I'd want to move towards designing them, not just using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the department's digital service team the first time a post opened. I'd volunteer to help roll out the new tools in our branch, write the guidance, run the training. And I'd keep going to union meetings, because someone who knows the tools should be in the room when they negotiate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. My bit of the world is changing and I'd like a hand on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're in a union but you like the tools. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easily, I think. A union that doesn't understand the software will lose every argument about it, so I'd rather be the member who does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra on the front desk, she's been there twenty years and she hates the screens. She's brilliant with people. I'd worry they'd see her as slow instead of seeing what she's good at.

say: I'd call it a chance to **fix boring work** and see claimants more.
I'd insist the **savings go back** into the service, not into cuts.
think: I'm **better placed** than most juniors because colleagues already rely on me.
Using tools won't save me, so I'd move towards **designing them**.
do: Apply to the **digital service team** when a post opens.
Run the **branch rollout**, writing guidance and training colleagues.
Keep attending **union meetings** to advise on the tools.
S1.quote: A union that doesn't understand the software will lose every argument about it, so I'd rather be the member who does.
fieldNote: He sees no conflict between **union loyalty** and enthusiasm for AI.
He knows tool skills **aren't protection** if tools do the whole job.
He worries for older colleagues like Sandra whose **people skills** may be undervalued.

steps.text: Apply for the department's digital service team
Run the AI tool rollout and training at Harbour Street
Advise the union branch on the new tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's a different feeling. Two years is nothing in government. A form takes two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs an emergency plan, like a pandemic plan: income support for everyone whose job goes, starting before they go. I'd be posting about it every day, probably annoying people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the digital team plan wouldn't save me either. If AI can design services as well as people, the department doesn't need a junior who's good at prompts. My whole job is screen work, so I'm hit in 2028, not 2031. Tomas is the lucky one, his work is hands-on, so he gets till about 2031 at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get our savings from four to six months fast, by selling the car and cycling. I'd start doing paid weekend work helping local charities set up AI tools, while that's still something people pay for. And I'd go hard on politics, joining a campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've got skills that matter right now and a partner with three more years. But anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't helping charities with AI just speeding up the thing that's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but they'd do it anyway, worse, with someone selling them rubbish. I'd rather they had someone on their side. And it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomas say to each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That for a few years he's the earner and I'm the one with time. My boyfriend Tomas fixes knees with his hands, so for three years he'd carry us while I work out what's next.

say: I'd demand an **emergency plan** with income support starting before jobs go.
I'd post **every day** about it, even if it annoys people.
think: Even the **digital team** wouldn't save a junior who's good at prompts.
My screen work is hit in **2028**, while my partner's hands-on job lasts longer.
do: Sell the **car** and cycle to push savings to six months.
Do paid **weekend work** setting up AI for local charities.
Join a campaign for a **basic income**.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicked, thanks to useful skills and his partner's job.
S2.quote: My boyfriend Tomas fixes knees with his hands, so for three years he'd carry us while I work out what's next.
fieldNote: He judges his work as **pure screen work**, so the stated date applies directly.
His partner's **hands-on job** gives the household three extra years.
He turns his AI skill into a **short-term income** while it still sells.

steps.text: Sell the old car and cycle to work
Charge local charities for weekend AI set-up help
Join a basic income campaign and post daily

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get somewhere new, if you pick right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say use the warning to retrain people properly, with pay, starting with the most exposed jobs, which includes mine. I'd say it at the union and I'd say it to my MP's office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time to move one step away from the screen. The bits AI is worst at are sitting with someone who's scared and helping them decide. I'd want a job that's mostly that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time course in careers guidance, the face-to-face kind. I'd keep using the AI tools at work so I stay useful in the meantime. And I'd talk to Tomas about moving to the city, where there'd be more of those roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but busy. Five years is enough to try something, and maybe fail once, and try again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Careers guidance is still thinking work. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's people at the worst moment of their working life. A man who's just lost his job at the fish plant doesn't want a chatbot, he wants someone who's met his town. That might buy me more than five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving to the city be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Tomas, yes, he loves the hospital here. We'd have to choose whose work leads. We're not married, so it's an honest conversation about whose career matters more.

say: I'd ask for **paid retraining** starting with the most exposed jobs.
I'd raise it at the **union** and with my MP's office.
think: I'd have time to move **one step away** from the screen.
AI is weakest at **helping scared people** decide, so I'd aim there.
do: Start a part-time **careers guidance** course in year one.
Keep using **AI tools** at work to stay useful meanwhile.
Discuss **moving to the city** with my partner for more roles.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, with room to try, fail once and try again.
S3.quote: A man who's just lost his job at the fish plant doesn't want a chatbot, he wants someone who's met his town.
fieldNote: He aims for **face-to-face** work, even though it is still thinking work.
A move to the city raises **whose career leads** in his relationship.
He frames five years as room for **one failure** and a second try.

steps.text: Start a part-time careers guidance course next year
Keep using the AI assistant on every claim
Talk with Tomas about moving to the city for more roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a whole second career. I'd honestly see that as an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this right, so let's not waste it. A transition fund, a right to retrain, and the savings shared out. I'd be the cheerful one at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably do well for most of that decade. But the end point is the same: AI that can do almost any thinking work, including the job I'd move into. So I'd want something with real human trust in it, and some money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the careers guidance course slowly and still apply for the digital team. I'd start putting fifty a month into an index fund, so we're not only relying on wages by the end. And I'd keep using every new tool, because the people who understand them will be needed for most of that decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. Ten years is a long time to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you'd most want to avoid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. The danger with ten years of warning is spending nine of them as the clever guy with the prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might get married, actually, and buy a flat. Tomas's work is safe till near 2039, so the mortgage would make sense with ten years. With two I'd never sign.

say: I'd say we have time to **do it right** and shouldn't waste it.
I'd push for a **transition fund**, a right to retrain and shared savings.
think: I'd do well for **most of the decade**, then face the same end point.
I'd want work with real **human trust** and some money put by.
do: Take the **careers guidance** course slowly while applying to the digital team.
Put **fifty a month** into an index fund.
Keep learning **every new tool** while that skill is in demand.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **hopeful** about ten useful years.
S4.quote: The danger with ten years of warning is spending nine of them as the clever guy with the prompts.
fieldNote: He sees **ten years** as a second career, not a threat.
He knows the **end point** still reaches the work he'd move into.
Longer warning makes a **mortgage and marriage** feel possible.

steps.text: Take the careers guidance course at a slower pace
Put fifty a month into an index fund
Keep learning each new AI tool the department brings in
Talk with Tomas about marrying and buying a flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is less time than our digital projects take to launch. What would help is income support that starts before people lose their jobs, not after, and a real right to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how people like me feel about being the keen one. Being first to learn the new tools feels like protection, but I know it only buys time, not safety.

headlineQuote: Being first to learn the new tools feels like protection, but I know it only buys time, not safety.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old** junior jobseeker allowance caseworker in a small seaside branch.
He uses AI **every day**, writes his own prompts, and is still learning the benefit rules.
He stays **calm** in AI Plateau and reaches **anxious** in the faster AGI pictures.
His partner Tomas's **hands-on physio job** gives the household extra years of security.
He mixes **union politics** with early adoption and aims for face-to-face guidance work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which is faster than government digital projects even launch.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** that starts before people lose jobs, plus a real right to retrain.
